title: Quake Forecaster
mission: Can you predict where the next big quake is most likely? Use real USGS data to find out.
intro: Each dot is a real big earthquake (magnitude 6 or more) from the USGS. The model learns from the 2016–2020 quakes, then forecasts which map squares will have a big quake in 2021–2025.
red: A red square means the model thinks a big quake is more likely there over the next few years. It does not mean a quake will happen on a certain date.
legend: Bright dots: 2021–2025 quakes the model tried to forecast. Faint dots: 2016–2020 quakes it learned from.
radLabel: How far the model looks around each map square
radWhy: Quakes cluster in long belts along plate boundaries. Looking at nearby squares follows a boundary and can catch more quakes. But it also spreads risk into the quiet middles of plates, which makes more false alarms.
cutLabel: Past quakes needed to call a square risky
cutWhy: A higher bar means the model only flags squares with many past quakes. That gives fewer false alarms but more misses. A lower bar catches more but gives more false alarms.

step1.lead: Step 1: Predict. First the model runs once with its starting settings. That run is your baseline: your first run, the one you compare against.

q.rad: In Step 2 you will make the model look farther around each square. What do you think will happen?
q.cut: In Step 2 you will make the model need more past quakes to call a square risky. What do you think will happen?

rad: Looking farther will catch more quakes and make more false alarms
Looking farther will catch fewer quakes and make fewer false alarms
cut: Needing more past quakes will catch more quakes and make more false alarms
Needing more past quakes will catch fewer quakes and make fewer false alarms
Needing more past quakes will change nothing

step1.button: Lock in my prediction and run the baseline

instruction.rad: Look at the map. Each bright dot is a real big earthquake. Pick what you think will happen when the model looks farther around each square.
instruction.cut: Look at the map. Each bright dot is a real big earthquake. Pick what you think will happen when the model needs more past quakes to call a square risky.

step2.lead: Step 2: Change the highlighted setting. Scientists change one thing at a time. That way they know what caused the change.

needOne.rad: Move the highlighted slider up so the model looks farther, then train.
needOne.cut: Move the highlighted slider up so the model needs more past quakes, then train.

step2.tooMany: You changed both settings. Put one back so only one is different from the baseline.

step3.lead: Step 3: See what changed. Compare your new run to the baseline.

rows.base: A model that always says "no quake"

step3.accNote: Accuracy can fool you. Most squares never have a big quake, so a model that always says "no quake" still scores high. Check what the model caught and missed, too.
step3.predWrong: Your prediction did not match. That is fine. Scientists learn from surprises.
step3.alwaysNoNote: The "always no quake" score never changes. It is the score for never saying quake at all. A useful model should do better than just saying no.
step3.predMixed: None of the three choices fit exactly. The change was mixed, and that is fine. Scientists learn from surprises.

outcomes.up_up: It caught more quakes and made more false alarms.
outcomes.down_down: It caught fewer quakes and made fewer false alarms.
outcomes.same_same: Nothing changed: same quakes caught, same false alarms.
outcomes.up_down: It caught more quakes AND made fewer false alarms. That is better on both counts.
outcomes.down_up: It caught fewer quakes AND made more false alarms. That is worse on both counts.
outcomes.up_same: It caught more quakes, and false alarms stayed the same.
outcomes.down_same: It caught fewer quakes, and false alarms stayed the same.
outcomes.same_up: Quakes caught stayed the same, but false alarms went up.
outcomes.same_down: Quakes caught stayed the same, and false alarms went down.

step4.lead: Step 4: Explain. Finish the sentence in your own words.
step4.starter: When I changed ___, the model ___ because ___.
step4.hint: No names. This stays only on this device.
step4.button: Save and see what we found out

findings.title: What you found out
points: Big quakes cluster along plate boundaries. That is why the red squares follow long belts on the map.
A forecast gives the likelihood of a quake over years. No one can name the exact date.

Some quakes happen far from any plate boundary, like the New Madrid Seismic Zone near Memphis. It had no magnitude 6 quakes in this data, so a model trained only on past big quakes cannot flag it. The risk there is still real.
The model misses some real quakes. With the starting settings, it misses the square with Hawaii. That square had only 1 big quake from 2016 to 2020, then another in 2021.
It also misses the square with the 2023 Turkey–Syria earthquakes. That square had 1 big quake from 2016 to 2020, then 8 from 2021 to 2025.

check.q: The model colors the square around a city red. What does that mean?
choices: A big quake is more likely there over the next few years
Correct. A forecast is about likelihood over time, not a date.
A big quake will happen there on a date the model knows
Squares that are not red are safe from quakes

misconceptions.exact: No one can predict the exact day of a quake. Scientists forecast the chance of one over many years.
misconceptions.safe: A square that isn't red can still have a quake. The model misses some.
misconceptions.weather: Weather doesn't cause quakes or volcanoes. They come from plates moving deep underground.

freePlay: Free play: change any settings and test as many times as you like. Your runs are listed below.
